Diligent
dĭl´i-gent
adj. (steady and careful in application; rendering Hebrew charuts, Greek spoudaios)
From Latin diligens, the present participle of diligere, to love, to choose out — so diligence is at root love applied to a task, not mere busyness.

Biblical Definition

Diligent describes sustained, attentive labour, and Proverbs makes it a whole doctrine of vocation. The diligent hand rules and enriches (Pro 12:24; Pro 10:4); the diligent soul is made fat (Pro 13:4); the diligent man's thoughts “tend only to plenteousness” while haste tends to want (Pro 21:5) — a distinction the modern hustle rarely observes. Diligence is not speed; it is steadiness under a chosen duty. Proverbs 22:29 promises it a hearing in high places: “Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings.” The word is not confined to commerce. Joshua commands diligent heed to the commandment and the law (Jos 22:5); the judges must make diligent inquisition before condemning (Deu 19:18); the psalmist makes diligent search of his own spirit in the night (Psa 77:6); and Peter commands the same energy in the soul's cultivation — “giving all diligence, add to your faith virtue” (2Pe 1:5). Diligence in Scripture is first applied to the heart, and only then to the herd.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines diligent as steady in application to business, constant in effort to accomplish what is undertaken, assiduous, attentive — and notes its Scriptural application to searching and to self-examination.

expand to see more

DIL´IGENT, a. Steady in application to business; constant in effort or exertion to accomplish what is undertaken; assiduous; attentive; industrious; not idle or negligent.

2. Steadily applied; prosecuted with care and constant effort; careful; assiduous; as diligent search or inquiry.

The hand of the diligent maketh rich. Prov. x.

Key Scripture

Pro 10:4 — "He becometh poor that dealeth with a slack hand: but the hand of the diligent maketh rich."

Pro 21:5 — "The thoughts of the diligent tend only to plenteousness; but of every one that is hasty only to want."

Pro 22:29 — "Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings; he shall not stand before mean men."

2Pe 1:5 — "And beside this, giving all diligence, add to your faith virtue; and to virtue knowledge;"

Modern Corruption

Diligence collapsed into hurry and self-promotion — the hustle that Proverbs 21:5 files under haste and assigns to want — while the diligence Scripture commands over the soul goes unpractised.

expand to see more

Proverbs 21:5 draws a line the productivity culture cannot see: the thoughts of the diligent tend to plenteousness, but of every one that is hasty only to want. Hurry mimics diligence and produces its opposite, because diligence is thoughtful continuance and haste is anxious motion. The man who works frantically and the man who works steadily are not doing the same thing at different speeds; they are doing different things, and Scripture assigns them different ends.

The deeper loss is the object. Peter commands all diligence toward faith, virtue, knowledge, temperance — the cultivation of the soul — and Proverbs 27:23 commands the shepherd to know the state of his flocks. Both assume that the things most worth tending are the things most easily neglected while a man is busy. A believer may be scrupulously diligent in his trade and entirely slack in his own heart, and Scripture counts that man slothful where it matters.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew charuts (H2742), sharp, decisive, diligent — literally something cut in, the opposite of a slack hand; Greek spoude (G4710), earnest haste, zeal — Peter's all diligence.

expand to see more

Hebrew charuts (H2742) — sharp, keen, diligent; set against remiyyah, the slack or deceitful hand (Pro 10:4).

Hebrew atsel (H6102) — the sluggard; Proverbs' standing foil to the diligent (Pro 13:4).

Greek spoude (G4710) — diligence, earnestness; giving all diligence in 2Pe 1:5, the soul's cultivation.

Usage

"“The hand of the diligent maketh rich” — steadiness, not brilliance, is the promise."

"“The thoughts of the diligent tend only to plenteousness” — and haste, only to want."

"“Giving all diligence, add to your faith virtue” — the soul is the first field."
